big: Meena lends ₹1,000 to a company for 5 years and is promised ₹80 every year. Is that a fixed 8% with no risk? Follow the money first, then the price tag.

lines: My bond pays a fixed 8% coupon. A bond gives a fixed rate, so there is no risk, right?
The coupon is fixed, yes. But a bond has a price too, and the price is not fixed. Let us watch one bond.

alt: Five bars showing four coupons of ₹80 and a last year of ₹80 plus ₹1,000
caps: A bond is a loan. Meena lends ₹1,000, the face value, for 5 years at an 8% coupon.
Each year the issuer pays 8% of ₹1,000, which is ₹80. The coupon is worked on face value, not on price.
In year 5 the last ₹80 arrives together with the ₹1,000 face value.
₹80 × 5 plus ₹1,000 is ₹1,400 back, if the issuer pays everything as promised.

alt: Two buyers pay different prices for the same bond and earn different yields
caps: The same bond, 5 years left, ₹80 coupon. One buyer pays ₹920 and another pays ₹1,080.
Both get ₹80 a year. The coupon cannot change, so only the price differs.
Paying ₹920 and getting ₹1,000 back gives a yield to maturity of about 10.1%.
Paying ₹1,080 for the same cash gives only about 6.1%.
Coupon fixed, price moves, yield moves.

title: What 'fixed' really fixes
stops: The coupon in rupees is fixed
alt: A shield with what a bond fixes and what it does not
caps: A bond fixes the coupon and the face value due back at maturity.
A government security carries the government's credit. A company bond carries the company's.
But the market price moves, and a company can miss a payment. Fixed does not mean no risk.

q: Meena's bond has a face value of ₹1,000 and a 7.5% coupon. She bought it in the market for ₹950. How much does the issuer pay her each year?
opts: ₹75 a year, as the coupon is 7.5% of face value
₹71.25 a year, as 7.5% of the ₹950 she paid
₹79 a year, as that is the yield on her ₹950
It moves with the price, so nobody can tell her
why: The coupon is a fixed share of face value, so 7.5% of ₹1,000 is ₹75, whatever price she paid for the bond.
The coupon is never worked on the price paid. A lower price changes her yield, not the rupees the issuer pays.
7.9% is the current yield (₹75 ÷ ₹950), a ratio. The issuer's payment is still ₹75; only the yield changes.
The coupon is set when the bond is issued and printed on it. The price moves and the yield with it; the coupon does not.

q: After bad news about a company, its 5-year bond with an ₹80 coupon and ₹1,000 face value trades at ₹800. Rohan says his return is still 8%. What is closer to the truth?
opts: Exactly 8%, because the coupon on a bond never changes
Lower than 8%, because a fall in the price cuts the yield
About 13.8% if all is paid, which signals the market's doubt
Zero until the price returns to ₹1,000, as interest waits for par
why: The coupon is fixed, but 8% is only what a ₹1,000 buyer earns. Paying less raises the yield, so 8% is wrong here.
A lower price raises the yield for a new buyer, because the same ₹80 and the ₹1,000 come back on less money.
He pays ₹800, gets ₹80 a year and ₹1,000 at the end, which is about 13.8%. The market wants this because it fears a default.
Interest is paid on dates, whatever the price. A fall in price does not suspend the coupon unless the issuer defaults.

q: A 10-year G-sec yields 7.1%. A company bond of the same tenor yields 8.6%. Meena sees the extra 1.5% as a bonus. What is the best reply?
opts: It is a bonus, since both bonds carry a fixed coupon for the same ten years
It covers inflation, which hits company bonds more than G-secs do
It exists because company bonds have a higher face value than G-secs
It pays for the company's credit risk, the chance of a missed payment
why: Both have fixed coupons, but only one is backed by the government. The same tenor does not mean the same risk.
Inflation hits both kinds of bond alike. The gap between them is mainly about who might not pay.
Face value is a printed amount and does not explain a yield gap. The gap is the price of credit risk.
The G-sec has sovereign credit. The company could miss a payment, so lenders ask for extra yield as compensation.

q: Meena may need ₹5 lakh in 2 years but is offered a bond that matures in 8 years. Her cousin says fixed rate means safe. What should the adviser point out?
opts: She cannot sell it before maturity, so the money would be stuck
In year 2 she would get the market price, possibly below face value
Her coupon would be cut if she sold the bond before maturity
She would get the ₹1,000 face value back whenever she sells
why: Bonds can be sold in the market. The real catch is the price she will receive, not whether a sale is allowed.
Face value is due only at maturity. Before that, the market price applies, and it can be lower after a rate rise.
The coupon is set by the issuer and does not change when she sells. The buyer simply gets the remaining coupons.
Face value is repaid at maturity only. A seller in year 2 gets the market price, which can be above or below it.

pts: The coupon is fixed. The price and the yield move.
A G-sec carries sovereign credit. A corporate bond carries the company's credit risk.
Fixed does not mean no risk: you can sell below face value, and a company can miss a payment.
